1960

January 1960

January
  1. Conservative movement · Goldwater · 1960 elections, Jan.Chicago, the Union League Club. Twenty-nine members of Manion’s Goldwater for President committee meet. Wannamaker, South Carolina’s new Republican chairman: its thirteen delegates ready for Goldwater, though they might back Nixon in public for a time. Manion’s plan for Goldwater’s book: his own imprint, Victor Publishing, 50,000 copies in March, bulk sales to friendly businesses.1 Bozell: Goldwater will not be nominated, but as few as fifty delegates for him would serve notice and lay the ground for 1964; money for a national appeal and three or four speakers on tour.2
    1. 1 Rick Perlstein, Before the Storm: Barry Goldwater and the Unmaking of the American Consensus 61 (2001).
    2. 2 Laura Jane Gifford, The Center Cannot Hold: The 1960 Presidential Election and the Rise of Modern Conservatism 114 (2009) (Bozell; a Goldwater for President meeting at Chicago, Jan. 23).
    To check: Manion to the committee’s members, Mar. 11, 1960, Clarence Manion Papers, Chicago Historical Society (cited by Rick Perlstein, Before the Storm: Barry Goldwater and the Unmaking of the American Consensus 61 n.1, for the meeting (2001)); “Abstract of Minutes Taken at Goldwater Meeting,” Jan. 23, 1960, Chicago, Barry Goldwater Papers, Arizona Historical Foundation (cited by Laura Jane Gifford, The Center Cannot Hold: The 1960 Presidential Election and the Rise of Modern Conservatism 114 n.59 (2009)). Check: the date; Perlstein sets the meeting after Jan. 23 and does not date it; Gifford, 114, dates a Goldwater for President meeting at Chicago Jan. 23 by its minutes. Check: Gifford, 150, 153, has Shorey State chairman, 1956–62, and Wannamaker elected national committeeman at the State convention of Mar. 26. Places: United States, Illinois, South Carolina, Chicago. Names: Manion, Goldwater, Nixon, Bozell.Conservative movement ⟩⟩Goldwater ⟩⟩1960 elections ⟩⟩□
  2. States and cities · Press and broadcasting, Jan.Chicago, a press conference in the Summerdale weeks. Daley to a photographer: “I’ll not have the mayor’s office turned into a circus or hippodrome”; to the City Hall reporters: “There are even crooked reporters, and I can spit on some of them right here!”Adam Cohen & Elizabeth Taylor, American Pharaoh: Mayor Richard J. Daley: His Battle for Chicago and the Nation 254 (2000). Check: the day. Places: United States, Illinois, Chicago. Names: Daley.⟨⟨ States and cities ⟩⟩Press and broadcasting ⟩⟩□
  3. States and cities, Jan.Chicago. Daley announces O’Connor’s resignation as police commissioner, for his gall bladder; a committee to find a successor under Orlando W. Wilson, dean of criminology at the University of California, McFetridge of the Chicago Federation of Labor among its members.Cohen & Taylor, American Pharaoh, 254–55. Check: the day; the committee sat twenty-eight days before Feb. 22 (255). Places: United States, Illinois, Chicago. Names: Daley.⟨⟨ States and cities ⟩⟩□
  4. States and cities · Governors, Jan.Chicago. Stratton, at a press conference in his Chicago office across from City Hall: he will take over the city’s police unless Daley “stops laughing and cleans up the mess himself — quickly”; Daley to give up the party’s chairmanship.Cohen & Taylor, American Pharaoh, 254. Check: the day. Places: United States, Illinois, Chicago. Names: Stratton, Daley.⟨⟨ States and cities ⟩⟩Governors ⟩⟩□
  5. States and cities, Jan.Chicago, the Summerdale scandal. Richard Morrison, a burglar of 23 in custody, in a confession of seventy-seven pages: twelve officers of the Summerdale district his partners for almost two years, the goods carried off in squad cars; four truckloads of stolen goods in their homes. Daley, back early from Florida: “the most shocking and disgraceful incident in the history of the Chicago Police Department.” O’Connor, the commissioner, takes charge; 130 of the district’s police questioned.Cohen & Taylor, American Pharaoh, 252–53. Check: the day. Places: United States, Illinois, Chicago. Names: Daley.⟨⟨ States and cities ⟩⟩□

February 1960

Monday, Feb. 22
  1. States and cities, Feb. 22Chicago. Daley’s search committee, after twenty-eight days in executive session at the University Club, ninety candidates considered and fifty-three interviewed, names its chairman, Wilson, police commissioner; the idea McFetridge’s. Stratton: Wilson “has a good reputation.” Adamowski, to Republican women: Daley holds him up “as a facade.”Cohen & Taylor, American Pharaoh, 255–56. Places: United States, Illinois, Chicago. Names: Stratton, Adamowski.⟨⟨ States and cities ⟩⟩□

  1. 1960 elections · Democratic Party, Sept. 7Chicago, the Medinah Temple, the Illinois Democratic convention, a crowd of some 5,000. Stevenson says he is “proud to campaign now with all my heart and strength across the country” for Kennedy. His prepared speech assailed “regional-minded Democrats” as allies of Eisenhower and the Republican “old Guard wing”; he omitted the passage but said afterward that he stood by it. The price of a Republican President with a Congress “bound to be Democratic” is “a continual stalemate”; he finds it hard to follow the reasoning that a “new liberal Nixon is disengaging from the old conservative Eisenhower.”“Stevenson Assails Democrats Who Aided G.O.P. in Congress,” New York Times, Sept. 8, 1960.   1. Cuban Missile Crisis: Warnings, Oct. 19Chicago · eveningChicago, the Sheraton-Blackstone, evening. Salinger tells Kennedy that Robert Allen and Paul Scott are to run a column on an invasion of Cuba and that Carleton Kent of the Chicago Sun-Times asks about a parachute unit alerted for a jump on Cuba.1 Kennedy: “Call Kent and tell him that report is all wrong. Salinger presses O’Donnell to let him in on what is happening.1 O’Donnell: “All I can tell you now is that the President may have to develop a cold tomorrow. Its members, by Hess and Broder’s account: Eisenhower, five of the Senate’s Republican leaders, seven of the House’s, five governors, the four living defeated nominees, five of the national committee, one State legislator.4 Bliss to the committee: “I am no modern miracle man, but I will work hard and try to do a job for you.”5 Goldwater introduces Nixon, by Nixon’s account: the man “who worked harder than any one person for the ticket.”6 Nixon master of ceremonies at the luncheon before the vote.7 In the executive committee, Jan. 21, Burch: “obviously this is more or less a forced resignation.” Bliss: “We have been shoved out onto the curb by the broad hips of Lyndon Johnson, and we have got to get back into the middle of the road.” Stagg of Louisiana: “if Adam Clayton Powell can vote in the same party as Richard Russell, I can vote in the same party with Jacob Javits.”8

  1. Civil disorders: After King’s death, Apr. 6–7Chicago’s West Side, rioting from Apr. 5.1 Acting Governor Shapiro asks for troops, Apr. 6; Executive Order 11404, Apr. 7.2 The dead in Chicago, 11 (Check the count).3 The Guard on the streets Apr. 6 cannot cope; that evening the mayor and the governor ask for federal troops, and Califano brings the proclamation to Johnson, who signs it lying in bed.   1. 1968 elections: Chicago, Aug. 1Washington · 12:00 p.m.The White House, noon. Mayor Daley lunches with Johnson, with Mrs. Johnson and Lynda sitting in. Daley “was giving Lyndon a sales talk about coming to Chicago”: the Democrats want to give him a rousing welcome. Johnson gives “little encouragement,” stopping “just short of a positive ‘No’.” Mrs. Johnson says she will do whatever he wants and has “no enthusiasm for going.” On the war, Mrs. Johnson sees, Daley “simply wants out”; Johnson cites Korea and tells of the candidates making “unofficial offers” while he bargains for peace, with his story of selling Daley a house for $20,000 and Mrs. Johnson and Lynda Bird following him to the door at $18,000 and $16,000: “What would you do?”Johnson, White House Diary, 697–98 (Lady Bird Johnson’s account). Daley’s attitude is Mrs. Johnson’s reading (“the Mayor’s attitude spoke eloquently of the growing concern”). They had been listening to a tape from Charles Robb in Vietnam.
